title: HDFC Bank AT1 Bond Nightmare Deepens as West Asia NRIs Renew Complaints Over $100 Million Losses
excerpt: About 70 NRI investors in the UAE and Bahrain have resurfaced grievances over Credit Suisse bonds sold between 2017 and 2019 that were later written down to zero.
body:
• Approximately 70 NRI investors in the UAE and Bahrain have renewed complaints against HDFC Bank over the alleged mis-selling of $100–120 million in Credit Suisse AT1 bonds between 2017 and 2019.
  • The bonds were marketed as safe, fixed-return investments with 10–13% yields but were written down to zero when Credit Suisse collapsed in March 2023, wiping out investors entirely.
  • The Dubai Financial Services Authority restricted HDFC Bank's DIFC branch from onboarding new clients since September 2025 over regulatory breaches.
  • The renewed complaints add to HDFC Bank's governance challenges, including the resignation of former chairman Atanu Chakraborty and multiple US securities fraud class action lawsuits.

HDFC Bank is facing a fresh wave of complaints from approximately 70 non-resident Indian investors in West Asia over the alleged mis-selling of Credit Suisse Additional Tier-1 bonds, marking the second major round of customer grievances from the region in recent years. The complaints pertain to a financial product sold between 2017 and 2019 that raised an estimated $100 million, according to reports.

The renewed grievances come as India's largest private lender is already grappling with US securities fraud class action lawsuits and governance questions that have pushed its stock near a 52-week low of ₹715.10, down sharply from a high of ₹1,020.50 reached in October 2025.

How the AT1 Bond Mis-selling Unfolded

The controversy centers on HDFC Bank's branches in the Dubai International Financial Centre and Bahrain, which primarily serve NRI clients managing foreign currency non-resident deposits. According to multiple investor accounts and regulatory filings, bank employees allegedly marketed high-risk Credit Suisse AT1 bonds to NRI customers as safe, capital-protected investments similar to fixed deposits, promising returns of 10–13%.

AT1 bonds are hybrid capital instruments designed to absorb losses during financial stress. They are perpetual, pay discretionary coupons, and can be written down or converted to equity if an issuer's capital ratio breaches regulatory thresholds. When the Swiss Financial Market Supervisory Authority wrote down approximately $17 billion of Credit Suisse AT1 bonds to zero during the bank's emergency acquisition by UBS in March 2023, HDFC Bank's NRI clients lost their entire investments.

"Something goes on for eight years, and suddenly we take an action."

— Atanu Chakraborty, Former Chairman, HDFC Bank

Investors have alleged that bank staff persuaded them to shift FCNR deposits from India to Bahrain, where the AT1 bonds were then sold without adequate risk disclosure. Some claimed they signed blank forms or had their net worth falsified to meet eligibility thresholds for professional investors. In at least one documented case, a customer's annual income was allegedly inflated from $40,000 to $140,000 to qualify for the bonds.

Regulatory Fallout and Executive Terminations

The Dubai Financial Services Authority imposed restrictions on HDFC Bank's DIFC branch in September 2025, barring it from onboarding new clients or offering new financial services. The regulator found that the branch was servicing customers who had not been properly onboarded and that there were systemic issues with client classification.

HDFC Bank terminated three senior executives in March 2026 following an internal investigation. Those fired included Sampath Kumar, group head of retail branch banking, along with Harsh Gupta, Executive Vice President for Middle East, Africa and NRI onshore business, and Payal Mandhyan, Senior Vice President. Gupta and Mandhyan had been suspended in January 2025 when the bank began its investigation. An additional 12 employees received penalties ranging from major to minor.

The bank's own Staff Accountability Report acknowledged that "a high number of regulatory breaches specific to dealing with non-onboarded customers in DIFC had been identified for a considerable amount of time."

Compounding Governance Concerns

The AT1 bond complaints are layered on top of a separate governance crisis at the bank. Former part-time Chairman Atanu Chakraborty resigned in March 2026, stating that "certain happenings and practices within the bank" he had observed over two years were "not in congruence with my personal values and ethics." He later told CNBC-TV18 that the AT1 bond mis-selling was a key bone of contention with management.

Multiple US law firms, including Kahn Swick & Foti, Levi & Korsinsky, Hagens Berman, and Faruqi & Faruqi, have filed securities fraud class action lawsuits alleging HDFC Bank disguised payments as marketing expenditure to offer above-market interest rates to the Maharashtra State Road Development Corporation. The class period spans July 2023 to May 2026, with an October 2026 deadline for lead plaintiff applications.

HDFC Bank commissioned an independent legal review by Wilson Sonsini Goodrich & Rosati and Wadia Ghandy & Co., which concluded there was no evidence to substantiate Chakraborty's allegations. The Reserve Bank of India stated it had "no material concerns on record" regarding the bank's governance.

What It Means for NRI Depositors

The case has raised broader questions about the protections available to NRI investors who place trust in Indian banks' overseas operations. With an estimated $100–120 million in exposure across the affected NRI client base, the scale of potential losses is significant. The Dubai regulator's intervention and the pattern of alleged onboarding violations suggest systemic issues rather than isolated incidents.

For the millions of Indian diaspora members who maintain financial ties with India through NRI banking products, the HDFC Bank saga underscores the risks of cross-border financial products and the importance of demanding full risk disclosures, particularly for complex instruments like AT1 bonds.

What Comes Next

HDFC Bank's stock has shed roughly 29% from its 52-week high, and the bank recently issued $1.75 billion in senior unsecured bonds through its GIFT City Branch. While the bond issuance signals underlying credit confidence, investors are watching closely for further developments in both the NRI complaints and the US class action lawsuits. The bank's board imposed a ₹100,000 penalty on CEO Sashidhar Jagdishan in July 2026 for his role in the MSRDC deposit pricing matter, characterizing the conduct as business overreach rather than personal gain.
